\section[\ar{الظهر} \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل}]{\ar{الظهر}, \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل} — noon and midnight}

\label{lesson:AR-C15-ad-duhr-muntasaf-al-layl}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Noon in Arabic isn't just a clock-time word — it's tied directly into the rhythm of daily prayer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{الظهر} — noon, and a prayer}
\textbf{\ar{الظهر}} (\emph{aẓ-ẓuhr} or \emph{adh-dhuhr}) = "\textbf{noon}" — from the root \textbf{\ar{ظ}-\ar{ه}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ẓ-h-r}), "\textbf{to appear, become visible}" (the sun standing at its highest, most visible point). Be honest about what makes this word different from Spanish's \emph{mediodía}: \textbf{\ar{الظهر} is also the name of the midday Islamic prayer}, \emph{ṣalāt al-ẓuhr}. For a Muslim, "noon" and "time for the noon prayer" are the same word — this isn't a neutral clock-time term the way "noon" or \emph{mediodía} are in cultures where the day isn't organized around five fixed prayer times.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل} — a transparent "half of the night"}
\textbf{\ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل}} (\emph{muntaṣaf al-layl}) = "\textbf{midnight}," literally "\textbf{the half of the night}." \textbf{\ar{منتصف}} (\emph{muntaṣaf}) comes from the root \textbf{\ar{ن}-\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}} (\emph{n-ṣ-f}), "\textbf{half}" (the same root as \textbf{\ar{نصف}}, \emph{niṣf}, "a half"), and \textbf{\ar{الليل}} (\emph{al-layl}) is simply "\textbf{the night}." This one is fully transparent — no erosion, no double meaning, just "the middle of the night," structurally exactly like Latin's \emph{media nox}.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "aẓ-ẓuhr" — noon, also the midday prayer{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "muntaṣaf al-layl" — literally "the half of the night"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest point — Arabic noon carries a religious meaning that mediodía doesn't{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ar{الظهر}} name besides the time of day? (\textbf{The midday Islamic prayer}, \emph{ṣalāt al-ẓuhr}.) What does \textbf{\ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل}} literally mean, and what root gives it "half"? ("\textbf{The half of the night}" — \emph{muntaṣaf}, from \textbf{\ar{ن}-\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}} \emph{n-ṣ-f}, "half.") Is Arabic's word for noon a neutral clock-time word the way Spanish's \emph{mediodía} is? (\textbf{No} — it's bound up with the daily prayer schedule.)
\end{tcolorbox}
